Chapter 4: Media, Violence, and the Shaping of Collective Memory
You know, the stories we see on the news, and the images that spread across our feeds, they don’t just inform us—they shape how we see ourselves and each other.
When violence erupts—let’s say a young man is shot by police, or a woman faces harassment on the street—suddenly, every detail gets picked apart and argued over. The victim’s entire life is put under a microscope, their choices questioned, and sometimes, their very humanity seems to be on trial.
For people who share the victim’s identity, these moments hit close to home. They aren’t just stories on a screen—they’re deeply personal. Each new report feels like a warning, a reminder that danger is never far away. And when these stories repeat, over and over, it starts to feel like violence isn’t just a possibility, but almost something you expect.
The role of the media in all this is... well, complicated. On one side, it shines a light on injustice, forcing us all to face tough realities we might rather ignore. But at the same time, it can turn real lives into mere headlines—stories that get boiled down to the most shocking details, rather than the full, complicated truth.
Too often, the focus sits on the spectacle, not the human being at the center of it all.
After violence strikes, there’s a sense of shared mourning. Communities come together—holding vigils, leading protests, raising their voices for justice. There’s pain, but also a fierce determination to be recognized and heard. These moments of unity are powerful. But let’s be honest—they’re also exhausting. It can feel like the cycle of violence and response just never stops, each new tragedy reopening the wounds from before.
That’s where art comes in. Through poetry, music, painting—people find ways to express what words alone can’t reach. These creative acts are more than just outlets for grief. They become forms of resistance—a way of saying, “We’re still here, and you won’t erase us.”
In the end, our collective memory is shaped by all these stories and images. For some, they become a rallying cry—a reason to stand up and push for change. For others, they’re a heavy weight, feeding fear or even despair.
The real challenge? It’s holding onto hope, and believing that a better future is within reach—even when the evidence sometimes says otherwise.
